cluster_name: TPLF offensive in Tigray prompts Ethiopia-Eritrea diplomatic break and regional alarm
event_summary: The TPLF launched a new offensive in northern Ethiopia on September 23, seizing airports; federal forces retook Mekelle's main airport by October 3. Ethiopia severed ties with Eritrea over alleged TPLF support and expelled an Egyptian diplomat, drawing reciprocal expulsions from both.
tldr: The headline layer splits into two clean registers: wire services, broadcast outlets, and Asian press lead with the federal military advance (airport retaken, rebels retreating), while African, European, and Gulf outlets foreground the Ethiopia-Eritrea diplomatic rupture and AU calls for restraint. Opinion outlets (Foreign Policy, The Conversation, African Arguments) add an alarm register — 'foretold war,' 'threatens to engulf' — absent from factual reporting titles. The structural drivers visible in body texts (Red Sea access, Nile dam disputes, Eritrea's port fears) are entirely absent from every headline in the corpus.

evidence.quote: Ethiopian army pushes back Tigrayan rebels
government forces retake airport from Tigray rebels

Addis Ababa as regional alliances fracture

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only headline in the corpus to treat the return to war as historically inevitable — 'Ethiopia's Foretold War Arrives' — using an editorial register absent from all factual reporting titles; this framing positions the conflict as predicted rather than sudden news.

Most geopolitically alarmist headline in the corpus — 'Threatens to Engulf the Horn of Africa' — uniquely frames the Ethiopia conflict as a regional conflagration risk rather than a bilateral or internal crisis.

Only headline to foreground fighting reaching the Ethiopian capital — 'Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned' — uniquely surfacing the threat to Addis Ababa at the homepage level where all other outlets kept coverage anchored to the Tigray frontline.

Only outlet to co-headline 'war' and 'diplomatic crisis' as parallel phenomena and to frame the conflict as Ethiopia being 'at odds with its neighbors' (plural) — uniquely casting this as a multi-neighbor rupture rather than the bilateral Ethiopia-Eritrea break that dominates all other diplomatic-register headlines.

bottom_line: Headline coverage splits into two clean registers — tactical military updates (airport battles, federal advance) dominant in wire and Asian press, and Ethiopia-Eritrea diplomatic rupture dominant in African and Gulf outlets — while the structural stakes of the conflict (Red Sea access, Nile dam water rights, unresolved 2022 Pretoria peace terms) that body texts develop as underlying drivers are entirely absent from every headline in the corpus.
